newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire war rivals jockey for position before talks.
newsitem.headline: Zaire war rivals jockey for position before talks.

text.p: Zaire's civil war rivals are jockeying for battlefield position ahead of a promised first round of formal talks which the United Nations says are tentatively scheduled for Saturday in South Africa.

With veteran President Mobutu Sese Seko and the Kinshasa authorities promising to name a negotiating team shortly, state radio on Monday reported fierce fighting around the rebel-held port of Moba on Lake Tanganyika.

Expatriates and traders in the southern mining capital of Lubumbashi said the Shaba province rail hub of Kamina -- a 24-hour rail journey from Lubumbashi itself -- had fallen to the rebels on Monday without a fight.

"In Kinshasa we should know within the coming days the names of the personalities who will make up the committee of negotiators," state radio said. "On the battlefield, the two sides are trying to increase pressure to have strong arguments at the negotiating table."
Laurent Kabila's rebels took up arms in October, vowing to topple Mobutu, who has dominated the sprawling former Belgian colony in Central Africa since a 1965 coup.

Mobutu, who had cancer surgery in Europe in August, has seen his grip on Zaire weaken as rebels have advanced west and south. Many Zaireans, weary and impoverished after three decades of his rule, are openly welcoming the rebel advances.

In New York, U.N. officials said the organisation's special Zaire envoy Mohamed Sahnoun would lead the talks in South Africa. Sahnoun also represents the Organisation of African Unity, which brought the two sides together last week in Togo.

The thorny question of a ceasefire date and the agenda remain to be worked out. Rebel spokesmen have said the first session will prepare a meeting between Mobutu and Kabila to discuss Mobutu's departure.
On the humanitarian front, the Tutsi-dominated rebels have told Rwandan Hutu refugees to move away from Zaire's third city Kisangani, which they captured on March 15.
They say the Hutus might include armed hardliners blamed for the 1994 genocide of minority Tutsis in Rwanda.
Aid officials hope to complete the move by Tuesday.
In the east, the U.N. refugee agency reported up to 30,000 Rwandan refugees arriving from the Masisi area at a village called Karuba west of Goma and saying they want to go home.
Ethnic Tutsis have been fighting Hutu hardliners in Masisi. Indigenous tribes in the hilly region also resent the intrusion of outsiders, saying they alone belong.
